reviewStatus: Drafted from verified sources; pending independent clinician review before clinical release.
name: Calculated Serum Osmolality and Osmolar Gap

version.label: Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose + urea (mmol/L)
version.detail: Equivalent to 2 × Na + glucose (mg/dL)/18 + BUN (mg/dL)/2.8. Osmolar gap = measured − calculated osmolality. Other formulas (e.g. 1.86 × Na) give different values and are not combined.

purpose: Calculates serum osmolality and the osmolar gap, e.g. when monitoring mannitol therapy.
intendedPopulation: Adults with serum sodium, glucose and urea results.

calculationMethod.share: Calculated osmolality {round(total)} mOsm/kg{isnull(meas) ? '' : '; measured ' + meas + ', gap ' + round(gap)}

resultStates.label: {round(total)} mOsm/kg
resultStates.detail: Typical reference range about 275–295 mOsm/kg; laboratories differ.

resultStates.label: Osmolar gap {round(gap)}
resultStates.summary: Measured osmolality exceeds the calculated value by more than 10 mOsm/kg.
resultStates.detail: Unmeasured osmoles (e.g. mannitol, alcohols) raise the gap; interpret with the clinical context and laboratory method.

clinicalContext.text: Used to monitor osmotherapy: a raised osmolar gap suggests mannitol accumulation.
Measured osmolality is needed for the gap; calculated osmolality alone does not detect mannitol.

clinicalInsights.text: Measured and calculated values should be from the same sample.

limitations.text: Formula-dependent; reference ranges and gap thresholds vary between laboratories.

limitations: Lipaemia and hyperproteinaemia affect sodium measurement.

confounders.effect: Raises measured osmolality and the gap.

whatItDoesNotTellYou: The cause of a raised gap.

guideSections.what: Calculated osmolality from sodium, glucose and urea, with the gap against measured osmolality.
guideSections.whenToUse: Osmotherapy monitoring and suspected toxic alcohol ingestion.
guideSections.howToPerform: Enter sodium, glucose and urea with their units; add measured osmolality for the gap.
guideSections.clinicalContext: Interpret with the laboratory's reference ranges.

sources.citation: Purssell RA, Lynd LD, Koga Y. The use of the osmole gap as a screening test for the presence of exogenous substances. Toxicol Rev. 2004;23(3):189-202.
